title: Details of the Assessment: Paper 1, Paper 2 and the Structure of Questions
summary: Understand exactly what each paper tests, how many questions students answer, how parts (a), (b) and (c) work, the timing and the advice for evaluation answers.

sections.h: Paper 1: Worship, Beliefs, Scriptures and Sacred Places
p: Paper 1 is a written paper.
• Time and marks: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks, 50% of the grade.
• Content tested: topics 1, 2 and 3 for each religion (Worship; Beliefs and scriptures; Sacred places).
• Christianity topics C1, C2, C3. Islam topics I1, I2, I3. Judaism topics J1, J2, J3.
• Sections: A Christianity, B Islam, C Judaism.
• Choice: candidates choose two of the three sections (the two religions they have studied). In each chosen section they answer two of three structured questions.
• Total: four questions, each worth 20 marks.
• Externally assessed (marked by Cambridge).

ex.t: Example: a candidate who studied Christianity and Judaism
b: Chooses Section A and Section C.
Answers two of three questions in Section A.
Answers two of three questions in Section C.
Total: four 20-mark questions = 80 marks.

sections.h: Paper 2: Festivals, Fasts, Family Life and Social Action
p: Paper 2 has the same format as Paper 1.
• Time and marks: 1 hour 45 minutes, 80 marks, 50% of the grade.
• Content tested: topics 4, 5 and 6 (Festivals and fasts; Rites of passage and religion and the family; Religion and social action).
• Christianity topics C4, C5, C6. Islam topics I4, I5, I6. Judaism topics J4, J5, J6.
• Sections A, B and C again. Candidates answer two of the three structured questions in each of their two chosen sections.
• Candidates should use the same two religions in both papers.
• Externally assessed.

b: Paper 1: places, people, beliefs and scriptures.
Paper 2: calendar, life events, family and action in society.
Both papers: same time, same marks, same structure, same AO weighting.

sections.h: Structure of every question: parts (a), (b) and (c)
p: Every question is worth 20 marks. Candidates answer all parts of the chosen question.
• Part (a): 6 marks. A short-answer question assessing AO1 Knowledge and understanding. It has two sub-parts, (i) and (ii). It usually asks for facts. One mark is awarded for each relevant point.
• Part (b): 6 marks. Assesses AO1. It usually needs a more detailed description and/or explanation. It is marked with the levels-of-response marking grid for AO1.

• Part (c): 8 marks. Assesses AO2 Evaluation, linked to the same overall topic. It needs a longer structured response that evaluates different points of view and gives a judgement. It is marked with the levels-of-response grid for AO2.
• Teachers should encourage students to look at the marks available when answering: a 2-mark part needs two points, not a paragraph.
• The balance is 12 marks of AO1 and 8 marks of AO2 in each question, so AO1 is 60% and AO2 is 40%.

ex.t: Time guide (a suggestion, not an official rule)
b: 105 minutes for four questions is about 26 minutes per question.
Part (a): about 5 minutes. Part (b): about 8 minutes. Part (c): about 12 minutes.
Leave 3 to 5 minutes at the end to check.

p: The syllabus gives clear advice about part (c). Teach it step by step.
• The question presents an issue where different points of view can be held.
• More than one point of view can be two opposing views (agree and disagree), but any views that differ from each other are enough.
• Answers must be in well-structured continuous prose, with paragraphs.
• Each paragraph states and then considers a point of view or argument.
• A point of view must be supported with evidence (a belief, teaching, practice or example).
• Answers should not be descriptive. They should focus on the specific question, not on broad themes linked to it.
• A firm, clear judgement: the examiner should see the position taken. The judgement should be reasoned and should build on the evidence before it.
• Candidates may draw on material from across the syllabus for that paper to present a range of arguments.
• Candidates are not penalised for using a different spelling to the syllabus, as long as it is clear which word they mean.

b: Point: state one view in a sentence.
Evidence: a teaching, belief or practice that supports it.
Explain: link the evidence to the question.
Link or counter: bring in a different view.
Judgement: end with a reasoned conclusion that answers the question.

sections.h: Marking: levels of response and specimen mark schemes
p: Parts (b) and (c) are marked with levels-of-response marking grids. The grids are published in the specimen mark schemes at www.cambridgeinternational.org/0490 and on the School Support Hub. Download them and read them before you start marking.
How levels of response work in general (the exact grid is in the specimen mark scheme):
• Examiners read the whole answer and decide which level describes it best.
• Then they choose a mark within the level, depending on how well the answer fits.
• Part (a) is marked point by point: one mark for each relevant point.
• For AO1, higher levels show accurate, detailed, well-developed knowledge and understanding with examples and links between ideas.
• For AO2, higher levels show clear arguments for different views, supported by evidence, with a well-reasoned judgement.
Important: Grade descriptions for this syllabus are not yet published. Use the specimen mark schemes.

b: Mark part (a) by counting valid points.
For (b), underline accurate facts and mark where explanation is missing.
For (c), highlight each view in one colour, evidence in another and the judgement in a third.
Share the grid with students so they know what is expected.

sections.h: Practical points: choosing questions, spelling and time
p: Teach these exam habits.
• Read the whole paper before choosing. Pick the two questions in each section where you can answer all parts.
• Do not choose a question because one part looks easy. All three parts count.
• Number answers clearly.
• Spelling: students are not penalised for using different spellings of religious terms (for example Qur'an or Koran), if it is clear which word is meant.
• Plan part (c) in three lines before writing: two views and a judgement.
• Write in paragraphs for (b) and (c). Bullet points may be used in part (a) if each point is clear.
• Use the vocabulary of the religion correctly and explain it.

b: Answering three questions in one section and one in another.
Choosing sections for religions they did not study.
Writing a long description in part (c) instead of evaluation.
Giving no judgement.

p: Check that students and teachers can answer these.
• How long is each paper, and how many marks?
• How many sections and questions do candidates answer?
• How are the 20 marks split?
• Which AO is tested in (a), (b) and (c)?
• What does a good part (c) include?
• Where are the levels-of-response grids?
Teacher tasks:
• Print the structure on one page and display it.
• Download the specimen papers and mark schemes.
• Plan three timed practice sessions: part (a) only, part (b) only and part (c) only.

b: State the marks for each part of a question.
Name the assessment objective for part (c).
Give two features of a well-structured evaluation answer.

activity: Make a one-page 'Exam at a Glance' sheet showing Paper 1 and Paper 2 side by side (time, marks, topics, sections, number of questions, parts (a), (b), (c), marks and AOs). Add a 10-line plan for a part (c) answer. Share it with students.

check.q: How many questions does a candidate answer in Paper 1?
o: Four, two in each of two chosen sections

check.q: Which part of a question assesses AO2 Evaluation?
Where are the levels-of-response marking grids published?

title: Command Words and Exam Technique: Worked Examples for Parts (a), (b) and (c)
summary: Learn the 11 command words with examples, and see model answers and marking notes for each part of a question, written for training and not taken from a Cambridge paper.

sections.h: What command words are and why they matter
p: Command words are the key verbs in a question. They tell the candidate what to do. If a student misreads the command word, the answer often earns few marks even when the knowledge is right.
• The syllabus lists 11 command words and gives each a meaning.
• The way a word is used depends on the subject context.
• Part (a) usually uses simple words (identify, state, give, outline).
• Part (b) usually uses describe or explain.
• Part (c) uses evaluation words, such as evaluate, assess, discuss, comment and compare.
Teach the words early and keep a poster on the wall.

b: Students circle the command word before writing.
Then write it in the margin with its meaning.
This takes five seconds and prevents the most common error.

sections.h: The 11 command words: meaning and example
p: Use these meanings from the syllabus. The examples are written for this course, not taken from a Cambridge paper.
• Assess: make an informed judgement. Example: 'Assess the importance of the Five Pillars for Muslims.'
• Comment: give an informed opinion. Example: 'Comment on the view that pilgrimage is a hard journey.'
• Compare: identify and comment on similarities and/or differences. Example: 'Compare the ways Christians celebrate Christmas and Easter.'
• Describe: state the points of a topic and give characteristics and main features. Example: 'Describe a synagogue service on Shabbat.'
• Discuss: write about issues or topics in depth in a structured way. Example: 'Discuss the role of the Pope.'
• Evaluate: judge or calculate the quality, importance, amount or value of something. Example: 'Evaluate the statement that fasting is the most important part of Ramadan.'
• Explain: set out purposes or reasons; make relationships between things clear; say why and/or how and support with relevant evidence. Example: 'Explain why Jews use a mezuzah.'
• Give: produce an answer from a given source or from recall or memory. Example: 'Give two names of Muslim charities.'
• Identify: name, select or recognise. Example: 'Identify two features of a mosque.'
• Outline: set out the main points. Example: 'Outline how Christians prepare for Easter.'
• State: express in clear terms. Example: 'State what Muslims mean by tawhid.'

b: Short recall: identify, state, give, outline.
Detail: describe, explain.
Judgement: assess, comment, compare, discuss, evaluate.

sections.h: Worked example: part (a) (6 marks, one mark for each relevant point)
p: Training question set (about Christianity, C1, written for this course, not a Cambridge question).
• Part (a) has two sub-parts, (i) and (ii), worth 6 marks in total. For training we use two sub-parts of 3 marks each.
• Training (a)(i): State three features of a church building. (3 marks) Model answer: altar, pulpit, font. (1 mark each)

• Training (a)(ii): Outline three things that happen at the Eucharist. (3 marks) Model answer: readings are said, prayers are offered, bread and wine are shared in memory of the Last Supper. (1 mark each)
Marking notes:
• One mark for each relevant point. Do not give extra marks for repeated points.
• A correct word without explanation can earn the mark if it answers the question.
• Students should stop when they have given the number of points the marks suggest.

b: Writing a long paragraph for a 2-mark sub-part.
Giving the same point twice in different words.
Not reading 'two' or 'three' in the question.

sections.h: Worked example: part (b) (6 marks, levels of response)
p: Training question: 'Explain why the Eucharist is important to Christians.' (6 marks)
Model answer (written for training):

'The Eucharist is important to Christians because it remembers the Last Supper, when Jesus shared bread and wine with his disciples and told them to do this in memory of him. By sharing bread and wine, Christians remember Jesus' death and sacrifice for them. For Catholics and Orthodox Christians the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ, so it is a very holy moment when they receive Christ. For many Protestants it is a way to remember Jesus and show unity with other believers. It is also important because the Eucharist brings the church community together every week, and reminds them of forgiveness and new life.'
Why this answer works:
• It gives several reasons, each explained (remembering the Last Supper, sacrifice, holy presence, community).
• It uses correct religious language.
• It includes different Christian views.
• It stays on the question.

b: Weak: 'It is important because Christians do it every Sunday.' (one point, no explanation)
Better: add why it is done (Jesus told them), what it means (sacrifice), and who believes what (Catholic and Protestant).

sections.h: Worked example: part (c) (8 marks, AO2 Evaluation)
p: Training question: ''The Bible is the most important part of Christian worship.' Evaluate this statement.' (8 marks)
Model answer (written for training):

'Some Christians would agree. Many Protestants believe the Bible is the word of God, so hearing it read and explained in the sermon is the heart of worship. For example, in many Baptist churches the sermon is the longest part of the service, because they believe God speaks to people through scripture. On the other hand, Catholic and Orthodox Christians stress the Eucharist as the centre of worship. They believe it is the most direct way to meet Jesus, and the Bible readings lead to it. Other Christians, such as Quakers, would say that silent waiting for the Holy Spirit is equally or more important, because they believe God can speak to anyone directly. In my judgement, the Bible is very important in all Christian worship because it shapes prayers, hymns and sermons, but it is not the only important part. Most Christians combine scripture, prayer and sacrament, so I think it is the most important for some, but not for all Christians.'
Why this answer works:
• It gives different views and says who holds them.
• Each view has evidence.
• It stays focused on the question.
• It ends with a firm, reasoned judgement.

ex.t: Marking checklist for part (c) (a classroom tool)
b: Two or more different views, each in its own paragraph.
Evidence for each view (belief, teaching or practice).
No unneeded description.
A clear judgement that follows from the evidence.

p: Use these training questions (not official) to practise.
Christianity:
• (b) Explain the importance of the Trinity for Christians.
• (c) 'Christmas has lost its true meaning.' Evaluate.
Islam:
• (b) Explain the importance of Hajj for Muslims.
• (c) 'Zakah is the most important Pillar of Islam.' Evaluate.
Judaism:
• (b) Explain why the Torah is important to Jews.
• (c) 'Keeping kashrut is essential for being Jewish.' Evaluate.
Teaching tips:
• Give students two minutes to plan and ten minutes to write.
• Mark with the checklist, then rewrite one paragraph.
• Share the best answers (with permission).

b: Two stars: what the answer did well.
One wish: what to add or change.
Check: did it give a judgement?

p: Common mistakes across all parts.
• Not using the command word.
• Writing in bullet points for (c).
• Describing instead of evaluating.
• Giving only one view.
• Forgetting to name denominations or traditions.
• Giving personal beliefs.
Revision plan for teachers and students:
• Week 1: command words poster and quiz.
• Week 2: part (a) practice on every topic.
• Week 3: part (b) explanations with peer marking.
• Week 4: part (c) plans for 12 statements.
• Week 5: timed full questions.
• Week 6: full timed papers and feedback.

b: State the meaning of 'explain' and of 'evaluate'.
Give two things a good part (c) must include.
Write one 'different views' sentence for a topic of your choice.

activity: Write one full training question set for one of your two religions, with part (a) (two sub-parts), part (b) and part (c). Write a model answer for each part, then mark a colleague's answer using the checklist. Add your set to your teacher file.

check.q: What does 'Explain' mean in the syllabus command words?
o: Set out reasons or make relationships clear, saying why and/or how, with evidence

check.q: Which part of a question needs a firm judgement?
How many marks does part (a) carry in each question?
